job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared flat with my cousin Layla, and I'm up early for a daily routine. First an hour of coding practice with an AI assistant explaining what I get wrong, then applications, then paid gigs cleaning datasets for a small online marketplace. I make about 400 pounds a month from that, which covers my half of the rent if I'm careful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did computer science with a data focus and passed with an average mark. My final project was a model that predicts which clinic patients will miss appointments, built with real anonymised numbers from a local clinic. I had no internship, and about 75 applications have brought three interviews and no offer yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, but I'd also say the plateau is probably a pause. At work I'd say the tools are a nice bonus. On social media I'd say use them for the boring parts and keep your own thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, it doesn't change my search much. Entry-level data jobs are competitive, and I'm one of hundreds with a pass degree. My cushion is a couple of months, and the freelance money is the only thing that makes it feel manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the freelancing and push it to 600 a month by taking one longer contract. I'd build two more project pages showing real results, like the clinic one, and apply to small firms and public bodies where a clinic project sounds relevant. I'd ask my cousin Layla to look at my CV, because she hires for a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, more than I expected. Not secure, but not shaky either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives you the okay feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm earning something and learning, even without an offer. A wage from freelancing makes me feel I'm not waiting, I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the sharpest worry underneath?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running out of runway before an offer comes. My cousin and I split a 700 pound rent, and my savings are about two months.

Use them for the boring parts and keep your own **thinking**.
think: Entry-level data jobs are competitive, and I'm one of hundreds with a **pass** degree.
My cushion is a couple of months, so freelance money keeps it **manageable**.
do: Push freelancing to **600 a month** with one longer contract.
Build two more **project pages** showing results like the clinic model.
Apply to small firms and **public bodies** where the clinic project sounds relevant.
feel: **Okay**, more than I expected; not secure, but not shaky.
S0.quote: A wage from freelancing makes me feel I'm not waiting, I'm doing.
fieldNote: Freelance **income** gives her agency that peers without it lack.
Her real fear is **runway**, with about two months of savings.
Uses AI as a **tutor** and keeps her own judgement.

steps.text: Take a longer freelance data cleaning contract to reach 600 a month
Build two more project pages with real results
Apply to small firms and public bodies with data needs
Ask cousin Layla to review the CV

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening, and the people who thrive will be the ones who can check and direct the systems. I'd say it online, I'd say it at the next meet-up, and I'd also say some people will get hurt and we shouldn't pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a squeeze, and I'm in the middle of it. The junior analyst jobs that used to teach people are being done by software, so there are fewer first rungs. I'm better placed than most, though, because I'm already working with the tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in what the tools can't fix easily, like messy real data, checking models and explaining results to people who aren't technical. I'd get a cloud data certification, around 300 pounds, and I'd pitch two small firms on a trial month. I'd also join a data community and swap leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and driven. I'd say stirred up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does checking a model actually involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Looking for mistakes that sound right. In my clinic project, the model was great at predicting who'd turn up and awful for patients who relied on one bus. I found that by looking at the actual mistakes, not the score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to people who don't use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They lose out quickly. I'd like to help my cousin Layla and others to see it, but I can't carry everyone.

say: The thriving people will be the ones who can **check** and direct the systems.
Some people will get **hurt**, and we shouldn't pretend otherwise.
think: Junior analyst jobs that taught people are being done by **software**, so there are fewer first rungs.
I'm better placed than most because I work with the tools **daily**.
do: Specialise in **messy data**, checking models and explaining results to non-technical people.
Take a cloud data **certification** for around 300 pounds.
Pitch two small firms on a **trial month**.
S1.quote: In my clinic project, the model was great at predicting who'd turn up and awful for patients who relied on one bus.
fieldNote: Her edge is **checking** results, shown with a concrete clinic example.
Sees fewer **first rungs** even for people better placed than most.
Wants to bring her **cousin** along but knows limits.

steps.text: Take a cloud data certification for around 300 pounds
Pitch two small firms on a paid trial month
Publish a write-up of the clinic model's errors
Apply for analyst roles that involve checking model results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move on retraining and income support now, and that we should be honest that nobody knows exactly how this will play out. I'd tell people not to hide from the tools, since that's not protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. My whole edge is that I'm good at working with AI, and if AI gets better than any human at thinking tasks, that edge disappears quickly. Two years doesn't give me time to build a business or a track record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on getting an income at once: stack up freelance work to cover rent for a year, even if it's tedious. I'd look at jobs where I help firms adopt the technology, since that's still a human job for a while. I'd save 300 a month, cut subscriptions and talk to Layla about moving to a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wobbly. I'd feel excited and sick at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the excitement come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curiosity. I'd want to see what it does. I just wouldn't want to watch it while my rent is unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about cheaper housing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Layla and I would find a smaller flat, maybe 100 each less. Or I'd move back with my parents for a year and save all of it, which I'd do if it gets bad.

say: Governments need to move on **retraining** and income support now.
People shouldn't hide from the tools, because that's not **protection**.
think: My edge is working with AI, and if AI beats any human at thinking tasks that edge **disappears**.
Two years doesn't give me time to build a **track record**.
do: Stack up **freelance** work to cover a year of rent, even if tedious.
Look for jobs helping firms **adopt** the technology.
Save **300 a month** and talk to Layla about a cheaper flat.
feel: **Wobbly**: excited and sick at the same time.
S2.quote: I'd want to see what it does. I just wouldn't want to watch it while my rent is unpaid.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** shows as curiosity, yet her edge is the first thing to erode.
Plans a **rent** buffer before any bigger move.
Has a **parental** fallback she would use only if things got bad.

steps.text: Stack freelance data contracts to cover a year of rent
Apply for roles helping firms adopt AI tools
Save 300 a month and cut subscriptions
Move to a smaller flat or back with her parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible, like fund retraining and make firms say where they use AI. I'd say that to friends, and I'd share what I learn publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels workable. If I get a first role within a year, I'd have years to move into more senior work, and I'm good at learning. It's still a race, but I think I can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first role in data or software even if it's not perfect, and grow into whatever the firm needs. I'd keep up the freelancing for the extra income, save 250 a month and put some into an index fund. I'd also try a few AI agent tools to see what they can do, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady and a bit keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the index fund be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A buffer for later. If work disappears and I don't have savings, I'm stuck. Even a small amount, put in regularly, is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about people who don't move as quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to bring them along, like my cousin Layla, with small steps. I won't pretend that's enough.

say: Five years is long enough to fund **retraining** and make firms say where they use AI.
think: It feels **workable**: a first role within a year gives me years to move up.
It's still a race, but I think I can **run** it.
do: Take a first role in **data** or software even if it's not perfect.
Keep **freelancing**, save 250 a month and put some into an index fund.
Try new AI **agent** tools so I'm not caught out.
S3.quote: If work disappears and I don't have savings, I'm stuck.
fieldNote: Treats the five years as a **race** she can run.

steps.text: Accept a first data or software role even if imperfect
Put 250 a month into savings and an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good amount of time, and we should use it to retrain people properly, with schools and workplaces involved. I'd say it positively, and I'd say it needs real plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I feel good about it. I could have a proper career, buy a place and maybe save for a home. The skills I'm building could grow with the tools, and that's a nice position to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a decent job, keep freelancing for a while and gradually move into a role that mixes technical skill with people skills. I'd study part time for a masters in data science if an employer helped, and I'd save a deposit. I'd also help my parents get comfortable with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit grateful, which feels odd to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why grateful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the time is a gift. Not everyone gets a decade, and I don't want to waste it. I've seen friends with no cushion and a lot less runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job hunt itself. A decade doesn't help if I can't get my first role. I'd still need one yes.

say: Ten years is a good amount of time to **retrain** people properly with schools and workplaces involved.

do: Get a decent **job** and keep freelancing for a while.

feel: **Calm** and a bit grateful, which feels odd to say.
S4.quote: Not everyone gets a decade, and I don't want to waste it.

steps.text: Take a decent first data job and keep freelancing a while

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my edge is working with the tools and that's the first thing to be replaced. With two years I couldn't build a track record. What would help is quick retraining that pays, firms hiring juniors who can show real projects, and honest information from governments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not special. I'm one of many graduates with a pass and a laptop, and the system should work for us as well as for the stars.

headlineQuote: I'm one of many graduates with a pass and a laptop, and the system should work for us as well as for the stars.
portrait: Yara is a 23-year-old **computing** graduate with a data focus, a pass, no internship and about 75 applications sent.
She shares a rented room with her cousin Layla and earns about 400 a month from **freelance** data cleaning.
She is centre-minded, uses AI every day and gets her confidence from **checking** what models get wrong.
Her mood is uneasy in gentle worlds, **anxious** when time is short and calm when she has a decade.
Her plan is income first, skills second and a **savings buffer**, with family as the last resort.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, because her edge is working with AI and that could be replaced first.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **paid retraining**, firms hiring juniors with real projects and honest government information.
